newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Assembly ends survey of world's hopes and fears.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Assembly ends survey of world's hopes and fears.

text.p: The General Assembly ended a 2 1/2 week general debate on Thursday after hearing representatives of 181 of the world body's 185 members, finishing a day ahead of schedule and saving -- at least on paper -- $81,600.
The annual debate serves as a barometer of the world's diplomatic climate, providing an opportunity for all U.N. members to discuss their hopes and fears.
Taking part were 12 heads of state, one crown prince (Albert of Monaco), 17 prime ministers, 17 deputy prime ministers, 106 foreign ministers, six other ministers and 22 ambassadors or other envoys.
Despite wide convergence in enumerating problems, agreement on answers proved more elusive.
As Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia put it: "If we appear to be able to gravitate towards common grounds of definition, we are not always clear or together on common courses of action."
Major topics included the need to reform the United Nations, restore its credibility and make it more relevant, he said.

This included ways of reforming and expanding the 15-nation Security Council and of ending the United Nations' perennial financial crisis. The organisation expects to end the year owed more than $2 billion in unpaid regular budget dues and peacekeeping assessments.

Many speeches touched on problems of development, debt, trade, finance and the environment as well as moves to eliminate nuclear weapons after the recent signing of a Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty by more than 120 countries.
Calls for a ban on the export of anti-personnel mines and for an end to the worldwide illicit arms trade also figured prominently.
Trouble spots which received particular attention ranged from the Middle East and the ethnically volatile Great Lakes region of Africa centring on Rwanda and Burundi, to the Balkans and Central Asia.
"There is a strong protest against silent armies of the night which bring chaos, despair and destitution to innocent people," Razali said.

A number of Caribbean countries warned of dire political and social consequences if their vital banana exports lost trade preferences now granted by the European Union but opposed by Latin America-based banana producers.

Several of the same countries also spoke out in favour of granting U.N. membership to Taiwan, even though the issue had already been smothered for the fourth year in a row by China and its supporters in the Assembly's steering committee.

With the United States threatening to veto a second five-year term for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the U.N. secretariat kept a close watch on how much support was expressed for him. One unofficial tally listed 32 speakers as backing his re-election.

Savings from ending a day ahead of time should serve as "a small but significant signal that we are seriously committed towards enhancing the efficiency of the U.N. and that we are tired of being bashed about by others outside," Razali said.
Much of the Assembly's work will now focus on its six main committees whose resolutions will later be referred to the plenary body for endorsement.
